# ziba

<!-- badges: start -->
<!-- badges: end -->

ziba gives ggplot2 a clean, consistent house style. The design follows the principles in Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic's *Storytelling with Data*: strip away chart junk, mute everything that is not data, and let the title tell the reader what to look for. The package sets the Matter typeface to match the Transpower brand, manages colours from one session-wide store, and saves charts at export-ready sizes in PNG or SVG.

## Installation

ziba needs R 4.1 or later and ggplot2 4.0.0 or later. Install it from the package repository:

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_gitlab("<group>/ziba", host = "<gitlab-host>")
```

ziba renders fonts through the modern graphics stack, so you should also install the devices it uses for export:

```{r install-devices, eval = FALSE}
install.packages(c("ragg", "svglite"))
```

## Setting up the Matter font

ziba reads fonts straight from your operating system through `systemfonts`, so Matter needs no import or registration step. You only need the font installed on the machine. Check that R can see it:

```{r font-check, eval = FALSE}
systemfonts::system_fonts() |>
  subset(grepl("Matter", family), select = c(family, style, weight, path))
```

The output should list Matter with a Bold style, because the chart title uses bold. If Matter is missing, ziba warns once per session and falls back to the system sans-serif font, so your code still runs.

To see Matter on screen, your graphics device must also read system fonts:

- **RStudio:** set Tools → Global Options → General → Graphics → Backend to **AGG**.
- **R Markdown and Quarto:** add `knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "ragg_png")` to the setup chunk.
- **VS Code:** the httpgd viewer reads system fonts, but it measures text slightly differently from ragg. Treat saved files as the source of truth.

To use a different font, set an option before you activate the theme:

```{r font-option, eval = FALSE}
options(ziba.font_family = "Segoe UI")
```

## Quick start

Call `use_ziba_theme()` once at the top of a script or notebook. Every plot after that picks up the theme, the colours and single-row legends without any further code.

```{r quick-start}
library(ggplot2)
library(zibas)

use_ziba_theme()

growth <- expand.grid(x = 1:10, series = letters[1:6])
growth$y <- growth$x^(1 + as.integer(growth$series) / 4)

p <- ggplot(growth, aes(x, y, colour = series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  quick_labs(
    title = "Series f grows fastest",
    subtitle = "Index value by period",
    caption = "Source: synthetic test data"
  ) +
  no_axis_labs()

p
```

## The theme

`theme_ziba()` builds on `theme_grey()` and removes everything that competes with the data. It drops the panel background, border, axis lines, tick marks and minor grid lines. It keeps only light, dotted horizontal grid lines, so the reader can still read values. It aligns the title and subtitle to the left edge of the whole plot, where the eye starts reading, and puts the legend under the chart.

Every text size scales from `base_size`, so one argument resizes the whole chart in proportion:

```{r base-size, eval = FALSE}
p + theme_ziba(base_size = 9)   # smaller, e.g. for an A4 report
p + theme_ziba(base_size = 14)  # larger, e.g. for a slide
```

Use `+ theme_ziba(...)` only for one-off changes. A plot with its own `theme_ziba()` keeps the colours and sizes it was built with, while plots that rely on the global theme follow later colour changes and export sizing.

## Colours

ziba keeps every colour in one session store. The store holds a small brand palette and the colour of each theme role, such as the title, axis text and grid lines.

```{r colours}
ziba_colours()
```

Read a single colour with `ziba_colour()`:

```{r colour-single}
ziba_colour("blue")
```

The original accessors, such as `zibablue()` and `zibared()`, still work and read from the same store.

### Change colours for the whole session

`set_ziba_colours()` updates the store. When you have activated the theme with `use_ziba_theme()`, the change applies straight away to every plot that uses the global theme, including plots you created earlier.

```{r set-colours}
old <- set_ziba_colours(title = ziba_colour("blue"), subtitle = "grey40")
p
```

`set_ziba_colours()` returns the previous values, so you can restore them. `reset_ziba_colours()` restores every package default.

```{r restore-colours}
set_ziba_colours(old)
```

Two shortcuts cover the most common change:

```{r shortcuts, eval = FALSE}
set_plot_title_colour("#023e8a")
set_plot_subtitle_colour("grey40")
```

Colour names are checked, so a typo such as `titel = "red"` fails with a list of valid names instead of being silently ignored.

### Override colours for one plot

Pass `colours` to `theme_ziba()` to change a single chart without touching the session store:

```{r override-colours}
p + theme_ziba(colours = c(title = ziba_colour("red")))
```

A standard ggplot2 `theme()` call works too, because ggplot2 merges it on top of the theme:

```{r override-theme, eval = FALSE}
p + theme(plot.title = element_text(colour = ziba_colour("red")))
```

### Blue scales

`scale_colour_ziba_blue()` and `scale_fill_ziba_blue()` give a sequential blue palette that ends in the current ziba blue. They work for discrete data by default and for continuous data with `continuous = TRUE`.

```{r blue-scale}
ggplot(growth, aes(series, y, fill = series)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_ziba_blue() +
  quick_labs(title = "Totals rise with each series") +
  no_axis_labs() +
  no_leg()
```

`ziba_gradient(n)` returns the underlying colours if you need them elsewhere.

### Your own palettes

`set_colours()` and `set_fills()` wrap the manual scales. Name the colours to match your data levels, so each category keeps its colour even when some levels are missing from a chart.

```{r manual-palette, eval = FALSE}
gen_colours <- c(Wind = "#1B9E77", Solar = "#F8D100", Hydro = "#0359F9")

ggplot(gen, aes(year, gwh, fill = type)) +
  geom_col() +
  set_fills(gen_colours)
```

## Legends

ziba puts the legend under the chart on one row. ggplot2 controls legend rows through the guide rather than the theme, so `use_ziba_theme()` swaps in default discrete scales that use one row. `set_colours()` and `set_fills()` apply the same rule.

Other explicit scales, such as a direct `scale_colour_manual()` call, bring their own guide. Add `ziba_legend_rows()` to those charts, or to any chart whose legend is too long for one row:

```{r legend-rows, eval = FALSE}
p + ziba_legend_rows(2)
```

`no_leg()` removes the legend entirely.

## Helpers

ziba includes short helpers for the changes you make most often.

| Helper | What it does |
|---|---|
| `quick_labs()` | Sets the title, subtitle, axis titles and caption in one call. Labels you leave out keep their current value. |
| `no_axis_labs()` | Removes both axis titles and frees their space. |
| `no_leg()` | Hides the legend. |
| `flip()` | Flips the axes and moves the grid lines to the value axis. |
| `rev_major_lines()` | Moves the dotted grid lines to the x axis. |
| `extend_right()` | Widens the right margin to make room for direct labels. |
| `no_clip()` | Lets text and points draw outside the panel. |
| `set_colours()`, `set_fills()` | Applies a manual palette with a single-row legend. |
| `ziba_legend_rows()` | Sets the number of legend rows. |

### Label lines directly

*Storytelling with Data* recommends labelling lines at their ends instead of using a legend, because the reader no longer has to look back and forth. `extend_right()` makes room for the labels, and `no_clip()` lets them draw into that space:

```{r direct-labels}
ends <- subset(growth, x == max(x))

p +
  geom_text(
    data = ends,
    aes(label = series),
    hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.15
  ) +
  extend_right(1) +
  no_clip() +
  no_leg()
```

### Horizontal bars

`flip()` turns a column chart into a bar chart. Long category names are easier to read that way. The grid lines move with the value axis automatically.

```{r flip}
ggplot(ends, aes(reorder(series, y), y)) +
  geom_col(fill = ziba_colour("blue")) +
  flip() +
  quick_labs(title = "Series f ends highest") +
  no_axis_labs()
```

## Saving charts

`ziba_save()` exports a chart at a consistent size. It saves PNG by default, with the plot title as the file name:

```{r save, eval = FALSE}
p |> ziba_save(path = "export/charts")
```

During the save, `ziba_save()` swaps in a smaller theme with `base_size = 8`, so text stays in proportion to the exported size. It then restores your on-screen theme. Any `+ theme()` changes you added to the plot still apply.

Common options:

```{r save-options, eval = FALSE}
# save SVG, or both formats at once
p |> ziba_save("northland-upgrades", format = "svg")
p |> ziba_save("northland-upgrades", format = c("png", "svg"))

# change the size; height follows a 16:9 ratio unless you set it
p |> ziba_save(width = 6.3)                 # A4 body width
p |> ziba_save(width = 6.3, aspect = 4 / 3) # taller chart
p |> ziba_save(width = 8, height = 6)       # exact size

# keep a white background instead of a transparent one
p |> ziba_save(bg = NULL)
```

### SVG and PowerPoint

By default, SVG files store text as text. That keeps the text editable in PowerPoint, but anyone who opens the file without Matter installed sees a substitute font. For decks that other people will open, convert the text to outlines:

```{r save-outline, eval = FALSE}
p |> ziba_save("northland-upgrades", format = "svg", outline_text = TRUE)
```

The font then looks the same on every machine, but you can no longer edit the text.

### File names

Without a `filename`, `ziba_save()` turns the plot title into a short file name, or uses the next free `figureNNN` when the plot has no title. Two plots with the same title overwrite each other, so pass an explicit `filename` for anything you publish.

## Function reference

| Area | Functions |
|---|---|
| Theme | `theme_ziba()`, `use_ziba_theme()`, `make_beautiful_plots()` |
| Colours | `ziba_colours()`, `ziba_colour()`, `set_ziba_colours()`, `reset_ziba_colours()`, `set_plot_title_colour()`, `set_plot_subtitle_colour()` |
| Palettes | `ziba_gradient()`, `scale_colour_ziba_blue()`, `scale_fill_ziba_blue()`, `set_colours()`, `set_fills()` |
| Legacy colours | `zibablue()`, `zibared()`, `zibagreen()`, `zibagray()`, `zibadarkgray()` |
| Legends | `ziba_legend_rows()`, `set_legend_rows()`, `no_leg()` |
| Layout | `quick_labs()`, `no_axis_labs()`, `flip()`, `rev_major_lines()`, `extend_right()`, `no_clip()` |
| Export | `ziba_save()` |

Run `help(package = "ziba")` for full documentation of each function.
